topic: Ellen and William Craft’s escape from slavery
centralQuestion: How did an enslaved couple escape openly—with the wife posing as a slaveholder and her husband as her slave?
thesis: The Crafts sustained an inverted social presentation by adapting to signature and conversation vulnerabilities; ownership scrutiny exposed its limits.
viewerPayoff: Understand two people’s strategy, the constraints it created, and the danger that survived arrival in the North.

sources.organization: William Craft / William Tweedie; UNC DocSouth transcription
sources.title: Running a Thousand Miles for Freedom (1860), first-edition pagination
sources.notes: Participant narrative twelve years after escape, narrated by William; primary testimony rather than independently observed checkpoint events. UNC proofed transcription with original pagination; title/frontispiece images identified. Exact dialogue, reconstructed emotions and surrounding anecdotes are not transcripts or adopted facts. Weekdays conflict with 1848 calendar; use December1848, not precise daily dates. The portrait omits facial poultice deliberately; it is a later portrait, not escape-day imagery.

sources.title: Singular Escape, letter dated January4,1849; issue January12,1849
sources.notes: Original issue header and enlarged article actually viewed. Near-contemporary abolitionist report after meeting the Crafts; not eyewitness observation of their journey. Information may come from the Crafts; early reporting is not independent travel corroboration. Its assertion they were out of reach in the North is contradicted by subsequent recapture attempts. Superlative unprecedented plan excluded.

sources.organization: Anonymous Daily Mercury correspondent; reproduced by Rosa Martinez / Cambridge University Press
sources.title: An Incident at the South (January19,1849), facsimile in Ellen Craft’s Spanish Masquerade (2023)
sources.notes: Inspected facsimile reproduced within scholarly article. Anonymous writer claims to have seen travelers aboard GeneralClinch and identified them after reading Brown. Additional perspective on presentation, with retrospective identification influenced by prior report. Original standalone microfilm not acquired; this is scholarly reproduced facsimile. Appended Brown extract is same source family, not extra corroboration. Spanish extraction is observer inference, not established intended ethnicity or a universal response. Literary readings and fictional appropriations are distinguished from historical action.

sources.title: Slave-Hunters in Boston!!, November1,1850, printed p.174
sources.notes: Original issue and enlarged article actually viewed. Contemporary Boston abolitionist reporting, independent of the later1860 memoir. Partisan rhetoric, numerical crowds and dramatic threats not used. Quoted Knight letter reproduced by newspaper is not its original manuscript. Does not establish every escape detail or all later travel dates.

sources.title: A Desperate Leap for Liberty: The Escape of William and Ellen Craft
sources.notes: Footnoted institutional synthesis; fine escape scenes mostly derive from memoir. Not an additional eyewitness. Daily route labels contain chronology/typographic errors, including1848January label. Baltimore bond-purchase wording oversimplifies memoir security demand; no universal statute asserted. Summary receipt retained as manual inspection, not full HTML body.

caveats.statement: Fine escape details derive mainly from their1860participant narrative. Early reporting supports inversion/signature strategy; traveling-correspondent facsimile supports appearance and William’s attendant role. Neither corroborates detailed Baltimore sequence independently. Exact dialogue, daily dates and universal travel rules omitted.

hooks.text: To escape slavery, Ellen Craft posed as a white male slaveholder. Her husband William posed as her enslaved servant.
hooks.viewerPromise: Explain how open travel exposed specific vulnerabilities and how they navigated them.

hooks.text: How could Ellen sign as a slaveholder when she could not write?
hooks.viewerPromise: Understand the functional disguise and its limits.
